source.title: Capability Scaling-Down Laws for LLM Compression
source.authors: Xue-Qi Cheng; Liang Wu; Kelly Wan; Liang-Jie Hong; Yu-Shun Dong

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; supplementary material referenced in the paper is not included.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies loss changes and prediction under compression, not held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameter count, tokens, or compute, nor compute-optimal allocation. Its references to pretraining scaling laws are background citations.
record.gate_note: The reported compression-loss results are a related but different construct. They do not test any listed claim version; selected findings are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study fits relations for loss change under pruning, quantization and distillation as functions of density, bit-width, group size, budget and reuse. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute. It does not test extrapolation of pretraining fits, compute-optimal allocation, shape effects at fixed size, or downstream predictability from pretraining scale. Kaplan et al. and Hoffmann et al. appear only as background citations in Related Work. Its power laws are in compression amount (1−d, or deleted capability mass), not in scale, so they do not bear on V5's scale-wise power-law form.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also conclude that the value of numerical prediction for selecting a compression method is small. On QA, a fixed method priority attains the same regret as numerical selection. The source-conditioned relations contribute measurement efficiency rather than better selection.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures pruning, quantization, and distillation responses rather than applying the original pretraining scaling-law methods.

fits_no_version.finding: After subtracting the measured first-order alignment term, pruning-loss curvature follows a power law in deleted capability mass. The exponent η concentrates in 1.2–2.2 across families, and a shared-η form transfers across families in leave-one-family-out tests.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compression-induced loss change follows a portable power law in deleted capability mass.

fits_no_version.finding: At 3 bits, per-channel round-to-nearest quantization collapses 12 of 14 models by 4.6–28 nats. OLMo-3 models are more robust.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compression severity varies strongly by model family, not by size alone.

fits_no_version.finding: A compact pruning form fitted on half the density grid matches the full-grid regression within 0.020 nats on math and code across Pythia, OLMo-2 and Wanda pruning. Coefficients must be refitted for each setting.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The shape of the compression response transfers across families and pruning criteria, while its scale does not.

fits_no_version.finding: Within Gemma-3 and Qwen3, robustness to pruning is not monotone in model size: Gemma-3 12B is the most robust size and 27B collapses earlier (Appendix C.1).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robustness to compression does not scale monotonically with parameter count within a family.

record.problems: The study's evidence is limited to the stated compression implementations, evaluation distributions, and tested ranges; it does not directly bear on the listed pretraining scaling-law versions. Some supplementary analyses are referenced but not present in the supplied text.
record.rows_left_out: Other compression results, including per-model loss tables, distillation responses, and additional predictor comparisons, were left out because they do not test the listed pretraining-scaling claim versions.

untested.parts: Pretraining loss as a power law in parameters, tokens or compute is not measured.
Extrapolation of pretraining-loss fits from small to large runs is not tested. Size extrapolation of compression predictors (Pythia 6.9B) concerns compression response only.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and tokens is not studied.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count is not varied.
No scale-wise power law is fitted in other modalities or regimes. Distillation and compression responses are fitted against reuse or density, not model or data scale.
Downstream accuracy is linked to loss only across pruned models (Appendix B, Table 17), not as a function of pretraining scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of pretraining-law exponents on setup is not tested. Setup dependence is shown only for compression coefficients, e.g. refitting across families and pruning criteria.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan 2020 and Hoffmann 2022 are cited only as background in Related Work. 'Scaling-down laws' here refers to compression responses, not to pretraining scaling. No row bears on any version.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out dense pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of dense pretraining-loss power laws from small to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation of parameters and training tokens.
Effects of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or nonstandard training regimes as stated in the version.
Downstream performance predictability from scale or pretraining loss.
Setup dependence or curvature of the original pretraining scaling laws and compute-optimal split.

rows.subject: Held-out battery
rows.operation_detail: Tested a compression-loss mechanism predictor using deleted capability mass after subtracting a measured alignment term.
rows.measure: Mean absolute error for the shared-η mechanism form versus raw sparsity and direct-damage baselines
rows.baseline: Raw sparsity: 10.3 nats; direct-damage baseline: 8.2 nats
rows.uncertainty: Both intervals excluding zero; interval values not stated
rows.note: Compression-response prediction, not prediction of dense pretraining loss.
rows.check: Link to none is correct. This is a post-hoc mechanism form (Appendix G.1) that uses the compressed model's gradient information. The authors call it an upper comparator, not a predictor. It concerns compression response, not pretraining scaling.

rows.subject: Heterogeneous panel
rows.size_stated: 12 models in the quantization table; text describes 14 models
rows.operation_detail: Measured capability-loss changes under per-channel round-to-nearest quantization.
rows.measure: Models described as collapsing and their loss-change range
rows.value: 12 of 14 models; losses of 4.6 to 28 nats
rows.note: The text reports this aggregate compression outcome; it does not measure a pretraining scaling law.
rows.check: Link to none is correct. Subject detail: Table 5 lists 14 models, the twelve-model panel plus Qwen3 8B and 14B. The range 4.6–28 nats covers the 12 collapsing models' capability losses at 3 bits.

rows.subject: Pythia, OLMo-2 and Pythia under Wanda pruning panels
rows.operation_detail: Compared a compact compression-loss predictor fitted with half the density measurements against a full-grid per-density regression.

conditions.value: three evaluations: Pythia magnitude pruning, OLMo-2 magnitude pruning, and Pythia Wanda pruning

rows.measure: Difference in mean absolute prediction error
rows.value: Compact relation matches within 0.020 nats per token on mathematics and code
rows.note: This aggregate is stated by the authors; coefficients are refitted for each evaluation. It concerns compression prediction, not pretraining-loss scaling.
rows.check: Link to none is correct. This compares the paper's own compact predictor with a full-grid regression, i.e. the study's method against an alternative. It does not test the claim.
